craft_claim: Grief is processed by oscillating between confronting loss and restoring ordinary life; unrelieved confrontation is maladaptive, so elegiac writing needs periodic recesses from mourning.

supporting_evidence.location: Death Studies 23(3):197-224, abstract and model description
supporting_evidence.note: The dual-process model identifies loss-oriented and restoration-oriented stressors and a dynamic oscillation between them, and argues explicitly for a dosage of grieving, with periodic respite, as part of adaptive coping.
Aesthetic distancing gives the recipient a sense of safety and control over continuing exposure, which allows negative emotion to be embraced rather than overwhelming.
Hedonic value is modelled as an inverted-U function of arousal potential; repetition of the same high-arousal material eventually lowers rather than sustains response.

counterevidence.note: A direct test failed to replicate a prolactin-based consolation response to sad music, so 'sadness is self-limiting because it feels good' cannot be asserted.

scope: All elegiac forms; the strongest warrant is for extended prose and sequences, where saturation is most visible.
exceptions: Short lyric elegies may legitimately sustain a single unbroken movement because they do not accumulate reader fatigue.
